kurals.tamil:
இடுக்கண் வருங்கால் நகுக அதனை
அடுத்தூர்வது அஃதொப்ப தில்.
kurals.transliteration:
Itukkan varungaal nakuka adhanai
Atuththoorvadhu aqdhoppa thil.
kurals.meaning: When trouble comes, meet it with a smile; nothing presses upon trouble and overpowers it as well as that cheerful calm does.
kurals.elementary: Imagine your sandcastle gets knocked over by a wave. You can cry, or you can laugh and start building again. The Kural says the laugh is the strongest tool you have: a cheerful heart beats trouble better than anything else.
kurals.university: The chapter opens with its most famous imperative, nakuka (laugh, smile), which the commentators do not read as mockery but as the outward sign of a mind that refuses to be shaken; Solomon Pappaiah paraphrases it as rejoicing inwardly, Mu. Varadarasanar as not being agitated. The second line turns on aṭuttūrvatu, literally ‘that which presses close and rides over’, a verbal noun describing what can close in on sorrow and subdue it, and aḥtoppatu il says nothing equals ‘that’ (the laughter or the unperturbed state it expresses). Parimelazhagar, whose commentary frames Idukkan Azhiyaamai as the natural sequel to the preceding chapter on sustained effort (Aalvinaiyudaimai), understands the troubles here as those that arise in the course of undertaking great works, so the king or doer must not lose heart midway. The couplet text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; ytamizh writes the chapter title as one word, இடுக்கணழியாமை, and thirukkural.net renders it ‘Not despairing in afflictive times’, while Pope’s title is ‘Hopefulness in Trouble’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O Dhritarashtra, thereafter, in the midst of both the armies, Shree Krishna smilingly spoke the following words to the grief-stricken Arjun.”
hinduism.explanation: At the darkest moment of the Mahabharata, with Arjuna collapsed in despair between two armies, Krishna answers him first with a smile (prahasann iva) before teaching him anything.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s first move against trouble is exactly Krishna’s: meet the crisis with a smile, and the smile itself begins the victory.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Striking parallel of smiling in the face of calamity, though it is Krishna smiling at Arjuna’s crisis rather than the sufferer smiling at his own.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations; Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience.”
christianity.explanation: James tells believers to greet their trials with joy, because hardship builds steadfast endurance in them.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, James makes joy the proper response to trouble and treats that joy as the force that wins through it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close: both command gladness at the arrival of trials; James adds a theological purpose (tested faith) the Kural does not state.

islam.quote_or_event: “For indeed, with hardship [will be] ease. Indeed, with hardship [will be] ease.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an twice assures the Prophet, in a time of pressure, that relief comes together with every difficulty.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s cheerful face toward trouble rests on the same conviction the sura repeats: hardship never comes alone and never has the last word.
islam._accuracy_note: Supplies the hopeful ground for laughing at trouble, but does not itself prescribe laughter or cheerfulness.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud tells of the sage Nachum Ish Gamzu, who met every misfortune that befell him with the words gam zu le-tovah, ‘this too is for the good’; when a gift he carried to the emperor was stolen and replaced with dirt, he still said it, and the dirt turned out to be miraculous.
judaism.explanation: Nachum became a byword for greeting each blow of fortune with serene confidence instead of lament, and his calm is shown to be vindicated.
judaism.tie_back: His habitual ‘this too is for the good’ is a Jewish form of the Kural’s smile at trouble, an inner stance that disarms misfortune.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match; the story grounds his calm in trust in God, while the Kural grounds it in strength of mind.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A mind unruffled by the vagaries of fortune, from sorrow freed, from defilements cleansed, from fear liberated — this is the greatest blessing.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Mangala Sutta the Buddha names a mind that stays untroubled through life’s ups and downs as one of the highest blessings a person can have.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural says an unshaken, cheerful mind is the strongest weapon against trouble; the Buddha calls that same mind the greatest blessing.
buddhism.source: Maha-mangala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 2.4 (tr. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the ideal of an unruffled mind amid misfortune, but lacks the Kural’s active image of laughing trouble down.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Heart, be still, you had worse than this to bear on the day when the terrible Cyclops ate your brave companions; yet you bore it in silence till your cunning got you safe out of the cave, though you made sure of being killed.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Back in his own house disguised as a beggar and surrounded by insults, Odysseus steadies himself by reminding his heart of worse troubles it has already survived.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus shows the Kural’s point that the mind’s own steadiness, not outward force, is what finally masters trouble.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Captures inner mastery of trouble, but Odysseus grits his teeth rather than laughs, so the cheerful tone of nakuka is missing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “for the mind converts and changes every hindrance to its activity into an aid; and so that which is a hindrance is made a furtherance to an act; and that which is an obstacle on the road helps us on this road.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius argues that a well-ordered mind can turn every obstacle into material for its own progress.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts hold that the right inner response does not just endure trouble but overpowers it and turns it to use.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on the mind defeating obstacles; the Stoic stresses rational conversion of hindrance rather than cheerful laughter.

kurals.tamil:
வெள்ளத் தனைய இடும்பை அறிவுடையான்
உள்ளத்தின் உள்ளக் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vellath thanaiya itumpai arivutaiyaan
Ullaththin ullak ketum.
kurals.meaning: Even a sorrow as vast as a flood is destroyed the moment a wise person turns a steady mind upon it.
kurals.elementary: Think of a huge wave rushing at a beach. It looks scary, but when it hits a strong rock it just breaks into foam. A wise, calm mind is like that rock: even a flood of problems falls apart when it meets clear, brave thinking.
kurals.university: The flood simile (veḷḷattaṉaiya, ‘flood-like’) stresses both the size and the sudden, overwhelming onrush of trouble (iṭumpai). The second line plays on uḷḷam (mind) and uḷḷa (to think, to resolve): the trouble perishes (keṭum) merely by the wise man’s mind thinking upon it, which Mu. Varadarasanar explains as reflecting on the nature of the trouble, and Solomon Pappaiah as the mind refusing to slacken. Parimelazhagar and later commentators read uḷḷam here as close to ūkkam, the mental elation or resolve praised in chapter 60, so that one act of firm resolve dissolves a whole flood of difficulty. The text agrees in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net, and Pope’s rendering (‘When wise men’s mind regards it, it is gone’) follows the same construal.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Having gained that state, one does not consider any attainment to be greater. Being thus established, one is not shaken even in the midst of the greatest calamity.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the yogi whose mind is settled in the Self as one whom even the heaviest sorrow (duḥkhena guruṇāpi) cannot move.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita and the Kural both place victory over the greatest affliction in the state of a steady, wise mind.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close in substance; the Gita speaks of a meditative attainment, the Kural of practical wisdom in worldly trouble.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus compares the person who hears and practises his teaching to a house on rock that survives the flood.
christianity.tie_back: Both use the flood as the picture of overwhelming trouble and say it breaks harmlessly on a well-founded mind.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shared flood imagery and survival through a firm foundation; the foundation in Matthew is obedience to Jesus’ words, not general wisdom.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah does not charge a soul except [with that within] its capacity.”
islam.explanation: The closing verses of al-Baqarah assure believers that no burden laid on them exceeds what they are able to bear.
islam.tie_back: The Kural says even a flood of sorrow can be undone by the wise mind; the Qur’an assures that no trial is truly beyond a person’s capacity.
islam._accuracy_note: Supports the idea that trouble is surmountable, but lacks the Kural’s emphasis on the mind’s own power to dissolve it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee, And through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee; When thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned, Neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah promises Israel that floods and fire will not overwhelm it, because God goes with it through every ordeal.
judaism.tie_back: Isaiah and the Kural share the image of a flood that cannot drown the one who meets it rightly.
judaism._accuracy_note: Same flood image and outcome, but safety comes from divine presence rather than from the sufferer’s own wisdom.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “By effort and heedfulness, discipline and self-mastery, let the wise one make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges the wise to build an inner island of discipline and mindfulness that no rising flood of passion or sorrow can cover.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts picture trouble as a flood and the wise person’s trained mind as the thing that survives it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near match in imagery and point; the Buddhist ‘flood’ (ogha) refers mainly to defilements rather than outward misfortune.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Zeus drowned the world in a great flood, only the pious Deucalion and Pyrrha survived; left alone on a devastated earth, they puzzled out the oracle’s riddle to throw ‘the bones of their mother’ behind them, understood it meant the stones of Mother Earth, and so repeopled the world.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s survivors of the flood overcome total catastrophe by keeping their heads and thinking their way to a solution.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, a literal flood of disaster is finally undone by a clear, thoughtful mind.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good image match; their rescue also depends on piety and divine favour, not wisdom alone.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius tells himself to meet misfortune like a headland that absorbs wave after wave without moving.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wise mind that dissolves a flood of sorrow is the same as Marcus’s promontory that calms the raging water.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close image of water broken by a firm mind; Marcus stresses endurance, the Kural the swift undoing of the trouble.

kurals.tamil:
இடும்பைக்கு இடும்பை படுப்பர் இடும்பைக்கு
இடும்பை படாஅ தவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Itumpaikku itumpai patuppar itumpaikku
Itumpai pataaa thavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who do not let sorrow grieve them turn the tables and bring grief upon sorrow itself.
kurals.elementary: A bully loves it when you get upset. If you stay calm and cheerful, the bully gets frustrated and gives up. Trouble is like that bully: if you refuse to be sad about it, the trouble is the one that ends up losing.
kurals.university: This couplet is a celebrated piece of Valluvar’s wordplay: iṭumpai (sorrow, affliction) occurs four times, arranged chiastically so that ‘those who do not suffer sorrow for sorrow’ are said to ‘cause sorrow to sorrow’. The form paṭā’a in the second line is an alapedai (metrical lengthening, அளபெடை), marked in thirukkural.net’s romanisation as paṭā'a and preserved in both sources consulted. The personification of trouble as an opponent who can itself be defeated recurs in 624 and 625, making the triad the rhetorical centre of the chapter; Parimelazhagar’s line of interpretation, followed by Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar, is that the undaunted person so frustrates misfortune that it withdraws defeated. Pope’s version, ‘From them griefs, put to grief, depart’, keeps the paronomasia.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O Arjun, noblest amongst men, that person who is not affected by happiness and distress, and remains steady in both, becomes eligible for liberation.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that the dhīra, the steady one whom pleasure and pain do not disturb (na vyathayanti), is fit for immortality.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s person who is not pained by pain is the Gita’s dhīra, and in both texts that refusal to be disturbed is what defeats suffering.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on not being pained by pain; the Gita’s reward is liberation, while the Kural’s is the rout of the trouble itself.

christianity.quote_or_event: “O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?”
christianity.explanation: Paul taunts death itself, the greatest affliction, declaring it has been robbed of its power.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul turns the tables on the enemy, so that the affliction becomes the defeated party.
christianity._accuracy_note: Same rhetorical reversal against suffering; Paul’s victory comes through resurrection faith rather than inner fortitude.

islam.quote_or_event: “So do not weaken and do not grieve, and you will be superior if you are [true] believers.”
islam.explanation: After the setback at Uhud, the Qur’an tells believers not to lose heart or sink into grief, promising that they will prevail.
islam.tie_back: The Kural and the Qur’an both link refusing to grieve with gaining the upper hand over misfortune.
islam._accuracy_note: Close: not grieving leads to superiority; the Qur’an conditions it on faith, the Kural on firmness of mind.

judaism.quote_or_event: “the days wherein the Jews had rest from their enemies, and the month which was turned unto them from sorrow to gladness, and from mourning into a good day; that they should make them days of feasting and gladness, and of sending portions one to another, and gifts to the poor.”
judaism.explanation: The Purim story ends with a total reversal: the decree meant to destroy the Jews recoils on its author, and their sorrow becomes celebration.
judaism.tie_back: Esther dramatizes the Kural’s reversal, in which the trouble meant to crush people is itself overturned.
judaism._accuracy_note: Captures the reversal of sorrow, but it comes through courageous action and providence rather than an inner refusal to grieve.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Throughout the Mara-samyutta, Mara the Evil One comes to the Buddha again and again in terrifying or tempting forms to shake him; each time the Buddha calmly recognizes him, and Mara, realizing he has been seen through, vanishes sad and disappointed.
buddhism.explanation: The personified force of affliction and temptation fails against a mind that will not be disturbed, and it is Mara who leaves dejected.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s paradox made into a story: the one who is not troubled by trouble leaves trouble itself defeated and grieving.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Excellent structural parallel of affliction itself being frustrated; Mara stands for defilement and death more than everyday misfortune.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Trapped in the Cyclops’ cave as Polyphemus devoured his men, Odysseus kept his head, called himself ‘Nobody’, blinded the giant and escaped under the rams, leaving Polyphemus roaring in pain that ‘Nobody’ was hurting him.
greek_mythology.explanation: The monster who meant to destroy Odysseus ends up the one in agony, outwitted by a man who did not panic.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus turns the Cyclops’ threat back on him, just as the Kural says the undaunted inflict trouble on trouble.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Vivid reversal story, though achieved by cunning and violence rather than the Kural’s simple refusal to be grieved.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that suffering comes from our judgments about events, so changing the judgment removes the disturbance.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s person who is not pained by pain has done what Epictetus urges, taking away trouble’s power over the mind.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Explains the mechanism behind the Kural’s claim, but lacks its striking image of trouble itself being defeated.

kurals.tamil:
மடுத்தவா யெல்லாம் பகடன்னான் உற்ற
இடுக்கண் இடர்ப்பாடு உடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Matuththavaa yellaam pakatannaan utra
Itukkan itarppaatu utaiththu.
kurals.meaning: The trouble that meets a person who, like an ox, keeps hauling the cart through every rut and mire will itself be the one that suffers.
kurals.elementary: Picture a strong ox pulling a heavy cart down a muddy road. Every time a wheel gets stuck, the ox just leans in and pulls harder until it’s free. If you keep going like that ox, your problems get tired before you do.
kurals.university: Maṭuttavāy ellām means ‘in all the places where (the cart) sinks or is blocked’, from maṭu, a pit or deep hollow, and the image is completed by pakaṭu, a draught ox or bull that pulls the cart out without flinching; Pope’s explanation renders pakaṭu as ‘buffalo … through deep mire’, reflecting a traditional alternative gloss for the animal. The second line again personifies trouble: the iṭukkaṇ that such a person meets ‘itself suffers hardship’ (iṭarppāṭu uṭaittu). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both stress persistence without losing heart, while Kalaignar expands the image into success through unbroken effort, linking this couplet to the doctrine of ūkkam and āḷviṉai in chapters 60 and 62. The text is the same in both sources; ytamizh prints the sandhi form மடுத்தவா யெல்லாம் exactly as thirukkural.net does.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Be steadfast in the performance of your duty, O Arjun, abandoning attachment to success and failure. Such equanimity is called Yog.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna asks Arjuna to keep doing his work steadily, unmoved by whether each step succeeds or fails.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ox that keeps pulling through every rut is a picture of the Gita’s steady, unattached worker.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares steadfast labour despite setbacks; the Gita stresses detachment from results, the Kural sheer perseverance.

christianity.quote_or_event: “No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the farmer’s plough to teach that once a task is begun, one must keep pressing forward without looking back.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts borrow the image of plough and draught animal to praise forward-pressing perseverance.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shared agricultural image of unwavering forward effort; Jesus’ subject is discipleship, not adversity as such.

islam.quote_or_event: “O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with [great] exertion and will meet it.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes human life as a hard, toiling journey (kadḥ) that nonetheless arrives at its destination.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ox straining through the mire, the Qur’an pictures life as exertion that pushes steadily to its goal.
islam._accuracy_note: Captures relentless toil toward an end, but says nothing of trouble being defeated; a next-best match.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you at liberty to neglect it;”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Tarfon teaches that one must keep at a vast task even when its completion is out of sight.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ox does not ask how long the road is; it keeps pulling, just as Tarfon forbids setting the burden down.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good on persistent labour; lacks the Kural’s specific claim that persistence defeats trouble.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Delight in heedfulness! Guard well your thoughts! Draw yourself out of this bog of evil, even as an elephant draws himself out of the mud.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses the image of a great elephant heaving itself out of a swamp to describe determined spiritual effort.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s ox dragging the cart out of the mire and the Dhammapada’s elephant pulling free of the mud are the same picture of strength against being stuck.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-identical animal-in-mire image; the Buddhist ‘bog’ is moral defilement rather than worldly obstacle.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Stranded in the Libyan desert, the Argonauts lifted the Argo onto their shoulders and carried it overland for twelve days and nights across the sand until they reached Lake Tritonis and could sail again.
greek_mythology.explanation: Instead of despairing when their ship could not float, the heroes became beasts of burden and hauled it through the obstacle.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ox dragging the cart through every rut, the Argonauts simply shoulder the load and haul it past the blockage.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good image of brute perseverance through a blocked road, though Apollonius credits divine guidance too.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus observes that when a lion attacks, it is the bull alone that knows its own strength and charges forward to protect the whole herd, using the bull as a model for the person who rises to hard circumstances.
philosophy.explanation: For Epictetus, difficulty reveals the strong character that is already in us, as danger reveals the bull’s power.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural too takes a bull as its model of strength that shows itself precisely when the road gets hard.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shared bovine emblem of strength under pressure; Epictetus’ bull confronts a foe rather than hauling through ruts.

kurals.tamil:
அடுக்கி வரினும் அழிவிலான் உற்ற
இடுக்கண் இடுக்கட் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Atukki varinum azhivilaan utra
Itukkan itukkat patum.
kurals.meaning: Even if troubles come piled one upon another, the troubles of a person who does not break inside are the ones that end up in trouble.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes bad things come in a row, like missing the bus, then spilling your lunch, then losing your pencil. If you keep your spirit strong and don’t give up, all those troubles run out of steam, one after another.
kurals.university: Aṭukki varinum, ‘even if they come stacked’, answers the natural objection to 623 and 624: what if troubles do not come singly but in a relentless series? The subject aḻivilāṉ is literally ‘one without destruction’, which Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss as one whose mind does not collapse (kalaṅkāmal, maṉam taḷarātavaṉ). The closing iṭukkaṇ iṭukkaṭ paṭum repeats the reversal of 623 with iṭukkaṇ instead of iṭumpai, the sandhi iṭukkaṭ reflecting the following p-. Both sources agree on the text, and the commentarial tradition treats 623-625 as a graded sequence: undaunted by one trouble, dragging through many ruts, and unbroken even by a pile of calamities.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Harishchandra, tested by the sage Vishvamitra, loses his kingdom, sells his wife and son, becomes a servant at a cremation ground, and at last must face his own son’s corpse, yet at every step he refuses to abandon truth; in the end the gods restore everything to him.
hinduism.explanation: The legend heaps calamity upon calamity on a single person to show a spirit that no accumulation of misfortune can break.
hinduism.tie_back: Harishchandra is the Kural’s aḻivilāṉ, the one whom troubles piled one on another cannot destroy, and who outlasts them all.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Excellent match for successive heaped troubles; the story’s explicit virtue is truthfulness more than cheerfulness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed;”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists affliction after affliction and after each one insists that it has not crushed him.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s ‘cast down, but not destroyed’ is almost a translation of the Kural’s aḻivilāṉ, the one troubles cannot destroy.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on multiplied troubles that fail to destroy; Paul attributes his resilience to God’s power.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits, but give good tidings to the patient, Who, when disaster strikes them, say, ‘Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns of a whole series of trials and promises good news to those who meet them with patient steadfastness (ṣabr).
islam.tie_back: Both texts expect troubles to come in numbers and give the final word to the one who remains unshaken.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on multiple trials and steadfastness; the Qur’an adds surrender to God, which the Kural does not mention.

judaism.quote_or_event: In the prologue of Job, messenger after messenger arrives, each still speaking when the next comes in: his oxen and asses are taken, his sheep burned, his camels seized, and finally his children killed; yet Job does not curse God or charge him with wrong.
judaism.explanation: Job is the classic figure of a man hit by calamities stacked one upon another who nevertheless is not broken.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘even if they come piled up’ is exactly the Job prologue, where disasters arrive faster than they can be absorbed.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close on heaped calamities; later chapters show Job in anguish, so the unbroken calm is only true of the prologue.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.”
buddhism.explanation: The wise person is compared to a rock that the storm beats against without moving it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s aḻivilāṉ is the Dhammapada’s rock, battered by repeated blows and unshaken by them.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good image of steadiness under repeated assault; the verse names praise and blame rather than calamity in general.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles is set labour after labour by Eurystheus, from the Nemean lion and the Hydra to the Augean stables and the descent for Cerberus, each harder than the last and some disallowed so that more had to be added, yet he completes them all.
greek_mythology.explanation: The labours are a mythic catalogue of troubles stacked one on another, deliberately designed to break him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Heracles is the Greek image of the Kural’s unbreakable one, whom an unending pile of trials only makes greater.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match on successive imposed trials; Heracles triumphs by strength more than by the inner calm the Kural praises.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Ignis aurum probat, miseria fortes viros.” (Fire tests gold, misfortune brave men.)
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that the gods expose good people to repeated hardships the way fire assays gold, to reveal and strengthen their worth.
philosophy.tie_back: For Seneca as for the Kural, a flood of misfortunes does not destroy the steadfast but proves them.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in spirit; Seneca stresses misfortune as a test, the Kural misfortune’s own defeat.

kurals.tamil:
அற்றேமென்று அல்லற் படுபவோ பெற்றேமென்று
ஓம்புதல் தேற்றா தவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Atremendru allar patupavo petremendru
Ompudhal thetraa thavar.
kurals.meaning: Would those who never clung anxiously to their wealth, saying ‘we have it’, ever wail ‘we have lost everything’ when it goes?
kurals.elementary: If you share your toys freely and don’t get too attached to them, you won’t cry much when one breaks. The Kural says people who didn’t cling to their riches don’t fall apart when the riches are gone.
kurals.university: The couplet sets two first-person plural verbs against each other: aṟṟēm, ‘we are bereft’, and peṟṟēm, ‘we have obtained’, the first the cry of the ruined man, the second the self-congratulation of the prosperous. Ōmputal tēṟṟātavar, ‘those who do not know (or care) to hoard and guard’, is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as those who did not greedily cling to wealth when they had it, while Solomon Pappaiah takes it as those who freely gave it away to others, and Kalaignar as those who were not elated by it; the three glosses share the idea that detachment in prosperity prevents despair in loss. The rhetorical question (paṭupavō, ‘would they suffer?’) expects the answer no, and the text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net. The couplet shifts the chapter from enduring trouble to preventing it inwardly, preparing for the equanimity teaching of 627-629.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A person who has given up all desires for sense gratification, who lives free from desires, who has given up all sense of proprietorship and is devoid of false ego – he alone can attain real peace.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that the one free of possessiveness (nirmama) and ego finds a peace that no loss can take away.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s person who never said ‘we have got it’ is the Gita’s nirmama, and that lack of possessiveness is why loss cannot make them wail.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.71 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close: absence of proprietorship leads to peace; the Gita frames it as a spiritual discipline rather than a worldly safeguard.

christianity.quote_or_event: “As sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes apostles who, holding nothing tightly, remain joyful even in poverty and grief.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s unclinging person who never cries ‘we are ruined’ matches Paul’s ‘having nothing, and yet possessing all things’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on joy without possessions; Paul’s paradox is rooted in spiritual riches, not in prior non-attachment to wealth.

islam.quote_or_event: “In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches believers to hold gains and losses lightly, neither boasting over the one nor despairing over the other.
islam.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s couplet in reverse order: no exulting ‘we have it’, and therefore no despairing ‘we have lost it’.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match linking lack of exultation in gain with lack of despair in loss.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines wealth as contentment with what one has rather than the amount one holds.
judaism.tie_back: A person who rejoices in his lot has nothing to wail over when fortune changes, just as the Kural says.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shared ideal of contentment; the Mishnah does not address the moment of loss directly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Happy indeed we live, we who possess nothing. Feeders on joy we shall be, like the Radiant Gods.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha, living without possessions, says his community is happy because it has nothing to lose.
buddhism.tie_back: Those who do not cling to what they own cannot be driven to despair by losing it; the Buddha’s joyful non-possession is the Kural’s point at its extreme.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Captures freedom from grief through non-possession; the Kural addresses lay wealth, the Dhammapada monastic renunciation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, an old Phrygian couple, lived in a humble cottage, making their poverty light by owning it openly and bearing it contentedly; when the disguised gods Zeus and Hermes came, they gladly gave them their best, and were rewarded.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s old couple are the model of people who neither clung to goods nor were embittered by lacking them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Their calm, generous poverty shows the Kural’s point: those who do not hoard do not despair when they have little.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good picture of contented non-attachment; the story concerns hospitality more than the experience of losing wealth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Never say of anything, ‘I have lost it’; but, ‘I have returned it.’ Is your child dead? It is returned. Is your wife dead? She is returned. Is your estate taken away? Well, and is not that likewise returned?”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that nothing external is truly ours, so its loss should be seen as giving back a loan.
philosophy.tie_back: Epictetus forbids the very cry the Kural mocks, ‘I have lost it’, by forbidding the possessive ‘I have it’ that comes before.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close: both trace grief in loss to possessiveness in gain.

kurals.tamil:
இலக்கம் உடம்பிடும்பைக் கென்று கலக்கத்தைக்
கையாறாக் கொள்ளாதாம் மேல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ilakkam utampitumpaik kendru kalakkaththaik
Kaiyaaraak kollaadhaam mel.
kurals.meaning: Knowing that the body is simply a target for pain, the noble do not treat the agitation it brings as a real calamity.
kurals.elementary: A football goal is made to have balls kicked at it; nobody is shocked when a ball hits it. The Kural says our bodies are a bit like that: bumps, colds and aches are bound to come, so wise people don’t panic when they do.
kurals.university: Ilakkam (from ilakku, ‘target’, cognate with Sanskrit lakṣya) makes the body the mark at which afflictions are aimed, an idea the commentators connect with the inevitability of bodily pain for every embodied being. Kalakkam is inner agitation, and kaiyāṟu is a rarer word that the traditional commentary takes as distress or helpless grief, so that the great ‘do not take agitation as (a cause of) distress’; Mu. Varadarasanar instead renders the construction as not adopting agitation as their way of conduct, showing a genuine interpretive divergence. Mēl, ‘the superior ones’, is the subject, with the verb in the honorific-epicene form koḷḷātām. The text is identical in both sources consulted, and Pope’s ‘Man’s frame is sorrow’s target, the noble mind reflects’ keeps the reasoning explicit.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Kunti, the contact between the senses and the sense objects gives rise to fleeting perceptions of happiness and distress. These are non-permanent, and come and go like the winter and summer seasons. O descendent of Bharat, one must learn to tolerate them without being disturbed.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna explains that bodily pleasure and pain are passing sensations like seasons, to be endured with titikṣā (forbearance).
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita and the Kural both hold that because bodily pain is natural and passing, the wise do not let it disturb the mind.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on the body as the natural seat of pain that must not agitate the mind.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.”
christianity.explanation: Paul accepts that the body is wearing away under hardship while the inner self keeps being renewed.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul separates the body, which takes the blows, from the inner person, who need not lose heart.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong body/inner-self distinction under suffering; Paul’s renewal is a work of grace.

islam.quote_or_event: “We have certainly created man into hardship.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an states plainly that toil and difficulty (kabad) are built into the human condition from creation.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s premise that the body is made to be a target of affliction, so hardship should not surprise or unsettle us.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the premise of inevitable hardship; the verse does not itself draw the conclusion about calm.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But man is born unto trouble, As the sparks fly upward.”
judaism.explanation: Job’s friend Eliphaz observes that trouble is as natural to human beings as rising sparks are to fire.
judaism.tie_back: Eliphaz states the Kural’s first line, that human life is a natural target for sorrow.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches the premise closely; Eliphaz is later rebuked in the book, and he does not draw the Kural’s lesson of calm.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sallatha Sutta the Buddha compares a painful bodily feeling to being struck by an arrow; the untaught person then adds a second arrow of mental distress by worrying and lamenting, while the well-taught disciple feels only the first, bodily arrow.
buddhism.explanation: Bodily pain is unavoidable, but the extra layer of mental agitation about it is optional and can be dropped.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s great ones accept the body as pain’s target yet refuse the kalakkam of the mind, exactly the Buddha’s refusal of the second arrow.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-identical teaching: bodily pain accepted, mental agitation over it declined.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles tells grieving Priam that two jars stand on Zeus’ threshold, one of evil gifts and one of good; Zeus gives some men a mixture and others only evil, so that no mortal escapes sorrow and all must endure what comes.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s image makes suffering a built-in portion of every human life handed out by the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles’ jars express the Kural’s premise that the embodied person is a natural target of trouble and should bear it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good on the inevitability of suffering; Homer’s tone is tragic resignation rather than the Kural’s serene refusal of agitation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Sickness is a hindrance to the body, but not to your ability to choose, unless that is your choice. Lameness is a hindrance to the leg, but not to your ability to choose.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus insists that bodily afflictions touch only the body, not the mind’s own power of choice.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts locate pain in the body and deny it any right to throw the mind into turmoil.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on the body as the site of harm and the mind as free of it.

kurals.tamil:
இன்பம் விழையான் இடும்பை இயல்பென்பான்
துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Inpam vizhaiyaan itumpai iyalpenpaan
Thunpam urudhal ilan.
kurals.meaning: One who does not chase after pleasure and who accepts hardship as a natural part of life never really falls into misery.
kurals.elementary: If you expect every day to be a party, a rainy day feels awful. But if you know that some days are rainy and that’s normal, you just grab an umbrella. The Kural says people who don’t demand fun all the time don’t get crushed when hard times come.
kurals.university: The couplet pairs two participial nouns, iṉpam viḻaiyāṉ, ‘one who does not crave pleasure’, and iṭumpai iyalpeṉpāṉ, ‘one who says hardship is natural (iyalpu)’, and concludes that such a person ‘has no falling into sorrow’ (tuṉpam uṟutal ilaṉ). Solomon Pappaiah restricts the pleasure in question to bodily pleasure, in line with 627’s focus on the body, while Kalaignar reads it more broadly as not roaming in search of enjoyment. The shift from iṭumpai (hardship, the event) to tuṉpam (suffering, the experience) is significant: hardship still comes, but it no longer becomes suffering. The text is the same in both sources, and Pope renders it ‘He seeks not joy, to sorrow man is born, he knows’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One whose mind remains undisturbed amidst misery, who does not crave for pleasure, and who is free from attachment, fear, and anger, is called a sage of steady wisdom.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna defines the sthita-prajña, the person of steady wisdom, as one who neither craves pleasure nor is shaken by misery.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita’s two conditions, no craving for pleasure and no disturbance in misery, are the two halves of this Kural.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match (sukheṣu vigata-spṛhaḥ / iṉpam viḻaiyāṉ; duḥkheṣv anudvigna / tuṉpam uṟutal ilaṉ).

christianity.quote_or_event: “These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples to expect tribulation as a normal part of life in the world, yet to stay cheerful.
christianity.tie_back: Jesus’ ‘ye shall have tribulation’ is the Kural’s iṭumpai iyalpu, and his ‘be of good cheer’ its promise that such a person is not undone.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on expecting trouble and staying cheerful; the peace offered is found ‘in me’, a Christological ground absent from the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do the people think that they will be left to say, ‘We believe’ and they will not be tried?”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns that trial is the normal, expected lot of anyone who claims faith.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, the verse teaches that hardship is part of life’s nature, so no one should be shocked into despair by it.
islam._accuracy_note: Affirms that hardship is to be expected; it does not address renouncing pleasure.

judaism.quote_or_event: “One is obligated to recite a blessing for the bad that befalls him just as he recites a blessing for the good that befalls him.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah requires Jews to bless God for misfortune as well as for good fortune, treating both as part of life’s ordinary course.
judaism.tie_back: Blessing the bad as one blesses the good is a ritual form of the Kural’s acceptance of hardship as natural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on accepting hardship; the Mishnah’s motive is devotion to God rather than protection from suffering.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces grief back to attachment to what is pleasing; without that attachment, grief has no root.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural says the one who does not crave pleasure does not fall into sorrow; the Dhammapada gives the reason, since sorrow grows from craving.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close causal teaching; the Buddhist target is attachment to the dear, slightly broader than the Kural’s craving for pleasure.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Offered ease and immortality on Calypso’s island, Odysseus chooses instead the hard road home to Ithaca, saying that if some god wrecks him on the sea he will bear it, since he has already endured much on land and sea and can add this to the rest.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus turns down endless pleasure and treats further hardship as simply part of his lot.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is the Kural’s man who does not crave pleasure and calls hardship natural, and so is not broken by it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match; Odysseus is driven by longing for home rather than a principled rejection of pleasure.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Nothing happens to any man which he is not formed by nature to bear.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius reminds himself that whatever befalls a human being is within human nature’s capacity to endure.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s view that hardship is iyalpu, natural to us, is Marcus’s view that we are formed by nature to bear it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on hardship as natural and bearable; Marcus does not mention renouncing pleasure.

kurals.tamil:
இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான் துன்பத்துள்
துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Inpaththul inpam vizhaiyaadhaan thunpaththul
Thunpam urudhal ilan.
kurals.meaning: One who does not greedily revel in pleasure when times are good will not be sunk in sorrow when times are bad.
kurals.elementary: If you jump up and down screaming when you win a game, you might cry just as hard when you lose. But if you enjoy the win calmly, you can handle the loss calmly too. The Kural says staying balanced in good times keeps you steady in bad times.
kurals.university: The couplet is built as a strict parallel, iṉpattuḷ iṉpam / tuṉpattuḷ tuṉpam, ‘in pleasure, pleasure’ and ‘in sorrow, sorrow’, so that the inner response mirrors the outer situation in each case. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the first half as not cherishing and clinging to pleasure when it comes, and Kalaignar summarises it with a Tamil jingle, not dancing in joy and not wilting in sorrow, as an example of regarding both alike. It differs from 628 in that it concerns one’s attitude within pleasure already present rather than the pursuit of pleasure. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net, and Pope’s ‘Mid joys he yields not heart to joys’ control’ captures the sense of inner restraint.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Established in God, having a firm understanding of divine knowledge and not hampered by delusion, they neither rejoice in getting something pleasant nor grieve on experiencing the unpleasant.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the knower of Brahman as one who neither exults (na prahṛṣyet) at the pleasant nor is shaken by the unpleasant.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita gives both halves of the Kural in the same order: no elation in pleasure, and so no grief in pain.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match of the paired attitudes to pleasure and pain.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says he has learned to stay the same person whether he has plenty or nothing.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s evenness in abundance and need is the Kural’s balance that refuses to be carried away in either direction.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on equanimity across fortune; Paul ties it to strength from Christ in the next verse.

islam.quote_or_event: “Strange are the ways of a believer for there is good in every affair of his … for if he has an occasion to feel delight, he thanks (God), thus there is a good for him in it, and if he gets into trouble and shows resignation (and endures it patiently), there is a good for him in it.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes the believer who meets good times with gratitude and bad times with patience, so that neither overturns him.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, the hadith prescribes a measured response in joy that makes a measured response in sorrow possible.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on balanced responses to joy and sorrow; the hadith frames them as gratitude and patience toward God.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider; God hath made even the one as well as the other, to the end that man should find nothing after him.”
judaism.explanation: Koheleth teaches that good and bad days both come from God, so neither should be treated as permanent or ultimate.
judaism.tie_back: Koheleth, like the Kural, pairs prosperity and adversity and asks for a measured, thoughtful response to each.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good on holding both conditions in view; Koheleth allows joy in prosperity where the Kural counsels restraint.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The good renounce (attachment for) everything. The virtuous do not prattle with a yearning for pleasures. The wise show no elation or depression when touched by happiness or sorrow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada describes the wise as neither lifted up by happiness nor cast down by sorrow.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘No elation or depression when touched by happiness or sorrow’ is almost a paraphrase of this Kural’s balanced pair.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on equanimity in both joy and sorrow.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Niobe, queen of Thebes, exulted so boastfully in her fourteen children that she set herself above the goddess Leto; when Apollo and Artemis struck them all down, her grief was so boundless that she turned to stone and weeps forever.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Niobe is the cautionary opposite of the Kural’s ideal: unrestrained delight in good fortune followed by unrestrained despair in loss.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Her story shows the Kural in reverse: one who revels without measure in joy is drowned without measure in sorrow.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A negative exemplum rather than a direct statement; her fall also punishes impiety toward the gods.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Consolation of Philosophy, Lady Philosophy shows Boethius that Fortune’s nature is to change, so whoever lets himself be lifted up by her gifts has already set himself up to be crushed when she withdraws them.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius learns that attachment to good fortune is what gives bad fortune its sting.
philosophy.tie_back: Philosophy teaches Boethius the Kural’s lesson: restraint in the enjoyment of good fortune is protection against despair in bad.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close argument; Boethius ultimately points beyond fortune to the highest good in God.

kurals.tamil:
இன்னாமை இன்பம் எனக்கொளின் ஆகுந்தன்
ஒன்னார் விழையுஞ் சிறப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Innaamai inpam enakkolin aakundhan
Onnaar vizhaiyunj chirappu.
kurals.meaning: If a person can take hardship as though it were pleasure, he will win a distinction that even his enemies will admire and desire.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a runner who smiles even while climbing the steepest hill in a race. Even the runners from the other team end up cheering for her. The Kural says if you can treat hard work and hard times as something good, even people who don’t like you will respect you.
kurals.university: Iṉṉāmai, ‘the unpleasant, pain’, is the negative of iṉṉā (sweet), so the couplet literally asks one to count the un-sweet as sweet (iṉpam eṉakkoḷiṉ). The reward is ciṟappu, eminence or distinction, qualified as oṉṉār viḻaiyum, ‘which even foes (oṉṉār, those not at one with us) desire or esteem’; ākuntaṉ is ākum taṉ with the final m assimilated, and viḻaiyuñ likewise before ciṟappu. Solomon Pappaiah specifies the hardship as that met while carrying out an undertaking, keeping the chapter’s Parimelazhagar-style link to the king’s or doer’s enterprise, while Mu. Varadarasanar reads it generally. The two sources agree on the text, and the couplet closes the chapter by turning the whole theme outward: inner mastery of trouble becomes public honour.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That which in the beginning may be just like poison but at the end is just like nectar and which awakens one to self-realization is said to be happiness in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that the highest kind of happiness often tastes bitter at first and only later proves sweet.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita’s poison-that-becomes-nectar is the Kural’s pain accepted as pleasure, which in the end yields true distinction.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.37 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close on counting initial pain as true pleasure; the Gita’s reward is self-realization rather than esteem from enemies.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ’s sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong.”
christianity.explanation: Paul declares that he actually takes pleasure in hardships, because through them he finds real strength.
christianity.tie_back: Paul does what the Kural commends, treating pain as pleasure, and finds in it a strength others cannot take away.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on taking pleasure in distress; Paul’s reward is Christ’s strength, not the admiration of foes.

islam.quote_or_event: “But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allāh knows, while you know not.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that what feels painful may in fact be good, since God sees its outcome.
islam.tie_back: The Kural asks us to count the painful as pleasant; the Qur’an explains why this can be wise, since the disliked may be the good.
islam._accuracy_note: Grounds the revaluation of pain; says nothing about winning honour or enemies’ esteem.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And as for you, ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.”
judaism.explanation: Joseph, once sold into slavery by his brothers, now rules Egypt and tells them the suffering they caused became the means of great good.
judaism.tie_back: Joseph treats his years of pain as a gift, and the brothers who once hated him now bow before his greatness, as the Kural predicts.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on hardship reinterpreted as good and on esteem from former foes; Joseph credits God’s plan rather than his own attitude.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though one may conquer a thousand times a thousand men in battle, yet he indeed is the noblest victor who conquers himself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says the greatest victory and honour belong to the one who masters his own mind.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s person who can turn pain into pleasure has won this inner victory, and it earns an honour that outshines conquest over enemies.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the theme of honour won through self-mastery, but does not speak of taking pain as pleasure.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At a crossroads, the young Heracles is approached by two women, Vice offering an easy life of pleasure and Virtue offering a hard road of toil; he chooses Virtue’s arduous path, which leads to lasting glory.
greek_mythology.explanation: Prodicus’ fable, retold by Xenophon, makes the willing embrace of hardship the way to true renown.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Heracles chooses toil as the Kural’s person counts pain as pleasure, and both win a fame the world must acknowledge.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good match of hardship embraced leading to glory; the enemies’ esteem in the Kural has no direct counterpart.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Nietzsche resolves to learn more and more to see what is necessary in things as beautiful, calling this amor fati, love of fate, and hoping one day to be only a Yes-sayer.
philosophy.explanation: Nietzsche’s ideal is not merely to endure hardship but to affirm and love it as part of one’s life.
philosophy.tie_back: Amor fati is a modern echo of the Kural’s counsel to take pain itself as pleasure.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on the revaluation of hardship; Nietzsche says nothing about esteem from enemies.

ytamizh-ch63.title: இடுக்கணழியாமை / Hopefulness in Trouble, Chapter 63 (Kurals 621-630) with Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Sivayogi Sivakumar commentaries
